title: The Treasury 'Debt Discharge' Myth — Where This Money Trick Really Began
summary: History of the redemption/debt-discharge myth from Roger Elvick and the 1980s farm crisis through HJR 192, the Montana Freemen and 18 USC 514, with the real kernel of fiat money.

assertions.quote: The treasury has stated flatly in published fraud alerts from its Bureau of the Fiscal Service that no such accounts exist

verdicts.note: Treasury: drafts and bills of exchange drawn on the Treasury are worthless, fraudulent and prosecuted; the accounts they draw on do not exist.

A homeowner's $244,663 'Bill of Exchange' drawn on a supposed IRS trust account was 'a worthless piece of paper'; the bank foreclosed lawfully, and the redemption guru she relied on was convicted of fraud.
A4V purports to pay from a fictitious government-operated bank account; Meads called it an 'unlocking spell' and the New Brunswick Court of Appeal in Bosse held the A4V scheme 'defies logic'.

Citing the 6th Circuit (Anderson), the Treasury does not maintain depository accounts against which an individual can draw; secret per-citizen accounts are 'pure fantasy' and fictitious instruments can be prosecuted under 18 USC 514.
The A4V money-for-nothing scheme (secret government account tied to the strawman) has been met by courts saying these ideas defy logic.

The NB Court of Appeal found an A4V scheme paying debts with 'setoff bonds' drawn on secret US Treasury accounts frivolous and illogical; the bills were 'obviously worthless' and the SCC refused leave.
FBI describes the strawman Treasury-account and 'accepted for value' redemption scheme as a method to defraud banks and the Treasury, amounting to extortion, not access to real funds.

assertions.quote: the paper is simply anti-counterfeiting stock and the numbers are ordinary vital records indexing
the redemption paperwork is not merely ineffective Congress wrote a specific felony around it and prosecutors use it regularly

verdicts.note: Treasury: these bills of exchange are worthless, using them is fraud and a violation of federal law, and the Justice Department has won convictions.
The court found the bill of exchange worthless, cited other courts finding the same, and noted the promoter and his co-defendants were convicted of fraud for passing such bills.
Money-for-nothing schemes (WeRe Bank cheques, Swissindo certificates, OPPT transfers) failed; OPPT guru Tucci-Jarraf was convicted of bank fraud and sentenced to 4 years 9 months.

1099-OIDs, bonded promissory notes and Treasury 'checks' are not payment of any debt; circuits upheld convictions for passing fictitious instruments (6th Cir. Heath, 8th Cir. Getzschman, 8th Cir. Johnson).
A string of Quebec bank cases rejected A4V debt discharge, supporting 'worthless'; the fraud prosecutions cited (e.g. Elvick) concern tax filings, not debt instruments.
A court found A4V setoff-bond debt payments worthless and frivolous, and said the users knew it; this passage does not cover fraud prosecution.
FBI calls redemption filings a fraud scheme against banks and the Treasury that leads to mail, bank, mortgage and wire fraud and tax charges.

assertions.quote: Money owed still had to be paid It simply had to be paid in federal reserve notes rather than gold

verdicts.note: HJR 192 declares US currency legal tender for all debts and measures obligations in dollars; the court says it addresses only the move off gold and supports no theory of discharge rather than payment.
Congress has declared Federal Reserve Notes legal tender (31 USC 5103), and circuits reject as frivolous the claim that they are not valid currency and are 'merely debts'; payment in them is lawful.
